title: 150 Effect of adopting multiple management technologies on cattle performance in a small grazing beef cow-calf system
content:
Abstract
This three-year experiment evaluated the effects of adopting several combined proven technologies on the performance of a grazing beef cow-calf system. A total of 108 Brangus cows were assigned to 1 of 2 cow-calf systems 1) high technology (HT; n = 46) or 2) low technology (LT; n = 62). Cows from each treatment were allocated to three groups and evaluated for 3 consecutive years using the criteria described in Table 1. All animals grazed bermudagrass during the spring/summer and ryegrass during the winter and supplemented with bermudagrass hay during the fall. Each HT replicate was stocked at 2 cows/ha, with priority grazing given to primiparous heifers and females with lower body condition scores (BCS), while LT replicates were continuously stocked at 1 cow/ha. HT females were synchronized for artificial insemination (AI) and exposed to a bull 14 d following AI. LT females were exposed to a bull for a 60 ± 5-d breeding season. Pregnancy rates were calculated using ultrasonography 42 ± 4 d following bull removal. BCS were recorded at calving for all females. Replacement females were retained for both HT and LT systems, with 50% of needed replacements being purchased for the HT system. Growth implants were placed in HT steers at d 60 ± 10 post-calving, and ionophores were fed through creep feed -70 d prior to weaning. Weaning occurred at an average d 205 ± 10 post-calving. Calf body weights (BW) were collected at d 60 ± 10 post-calving, -14 d prior to weaning and at weaning. Treatments did not affect (P = 0.74) the BCS of cows at calving, but HT vs. LT cows had greater pregnancy rates (treatment × year effect; P = 0.05) in yr 1 (82.1 vs. 64.9 ± 5.6%) and yr 2 (92.6 vs. 78.3% ± 5.6%), but not in yr 3 (83.3 vs. 88.1 ± 5.6%). Besides no effects of treatment on calf birth BW, HT vs. LT calves were heavier at weaning (treatment × day × year effect; P = 0.009) on yr 1 (275 vs. 245 ± 5.70 kg), yr 2 (297 vs. 247 ± 4.39 kg) and yr 3 (268 vs. 248 ± 3.86 kg). Interestingly, calf BW per cow exposed did not differ in yr 1 but tended to be greater (treatment × year effect; P = 0.09) in the HT vs. LT system in yr 2 (239 vs. 194 ± 18.2 kg/cow) and yr 3 (257 vs. 202 ± 18.2 kg/cow). Data suggests that implementing management technologies, including AI, growth implants, creep feeding with ionophores, and rotational grazing, can lead to improved calf performance for small beef cattle producers.
